stem: A company wants administrators to access EC2 instances without opening SSH port 22 or managing SSH keys.

options.text: AWS Systems Manager Session Manager
options.why: Session Manager provides browser or CLI shell access without open inbound ports or SSH keys.

options.text: A bastion host with port 22 open to the internet
options.why: This still requires open SSH ports and keys.

options.text: An IAM user with SSH access keys
options.why: IAM access keys sign AWS API calls; they don't replace SSH or close port 22.

options.text: EC2 Instance Connect with port 22 open
options.why: Instance Connect still uses SSH over port 22.

explanation.answer: Session Manager provides secure, auditable instance access with IAM-based permissions and no inbound ports.
explanation.concept: Session activity can be logged to CloudWatch Logs or Amazon S3.
explanation.examTip: Shell access without SSH ports or keys = Session Manager.

stem: An administrator wants answers to common AWS questions, such as how to fix a specific error, written by AWS.

options.text: AWS Pricing Calculator
options.why: The Pricing Calculator estimates costs, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: AWS Knowledge Center (on AWS re:Post)
options.why: The Knowledge Center has articles answering frequently asked questions.

options.text: AWS Artifact
options.why: Artifact provides compliance reports, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: AWS Marketplace
options.why: Marketplace sells third-party software, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

explanation.answer: The AWS Knowledge Center, part of AWS re:Post, contains articles and videos covering the most frequent questions and requests.
explanation.concept: AWS re:Post is the community Q&A site; the Knowledge Center has AWS-authored articles.
explanation.examTip: AWS-written answers to common questions = Knowledge Center.

stem: A Lambda function needs to read items from a DynamoDB table.
prompt: How should the function receive permissions?

options.text: Store an IAM user's access keys in an environment variable
options.why: Long-term keys in environment variables can leak.

options.text: Use the root user's credentials
options.why: Root credentials must not be used by applications.

options.text: Assign the function an execution role with DynamoDB read permissions
options.why: Lambda assumes its execution role and gets temporary credentials.

options.text: A DynamoDB resource policy allowing all principals
options.why: Allowing all principals is far too broad.

explanation.answer: Every Lambda function has an execution role that grants it permissions to AWS services through temporary credentials.
explanation.concept: Grant only the actions the function needs, such as dynamodb:GetItem on that table.
explanation.examTip: Lambda permissions = execution role.

stem: In IAM Identity Center, an administrator wants to give the Finance group read-only billing access in three accounts.
prompt: What should the administrator create and assign?

options.text: An IAM user in each account for each person
options.why: This is hard to manage and doesn't use Identity Center.

options.text: A security group allowing billing traffic
options.why: Security groups filter network traffic, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: A service control policy granting billing access
options.why: SCPs don't grant permissions, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: A permission set assigned to the group for those accounts
options.why: Permission sets define access levels that Identity Center provisions as roles in each account.

explanation.answer: IAM Identity Center permission sets define a collection of policies. Assigning them to users or groups in accounts creates the corresponding roles.
explanation.concept: This centralizes workforce permissions across accounts.
explanation.examTip: Identity Center access = permission set + group + account assignment.

stem: A company protects a web application with several layers.
prompt: Which TWO controls operate at different layers to provide defense in depth? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Using the root user for deployments
options.why: This weakens security, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: Security groups on the instances
options.why: Security groups filter network traffic at the instance level.

options.text: AWS WAF on the load balancer
options.why: WAF filters malicious web requests at the application layer.

options.text: Disabling CloudTrail
options.why: This removes audit visibility, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Sharing one IAM user among the team
options.why: Shared users remove accountability, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

explanation.answer: Defense in depth combines controls at multiple layers, such as AWS WAF (application), security groups (instance) and network ACLs (subnet).
explanation.concept: If one control fails, others still protect the workload.
explanation.examTip: Defense in depth = several independent layers of controls.

stem: A team asks whether Amazon Inspector or Amazon GuardDuty would tell them that an EC2 instance has an outdated, vulnerable version of OpenSSL.

options.text: Amazon Inspector
options.why: Inspector identifies known software vulnerabilities in packages.

options.text: AWS Artifact
options.why: Artifact provides compliance reports, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: AWS Shield
options.why: Shield protects against DDoS attacks, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: Amazon GuardDuty
options.why: GuardDuty detects suspicious activity, not outdated software packages.

explanation.answer: Amazon Inspector scans for known vulnerabilities (CVEs) in software installed on EC2 instances, container images and Lambda functions.
explanation.concept: GuardDuty looks at behavior; Inspector looks at software.
explanation.examTip: Vulnerable package = Inspector. Suspicious behavior = GuardDuty.

stem: A developer wants to ask the AWS community a question about configuring IAM policies and get answers from experts.

options.text: AWS Budgets
options.why: Budgets track cost, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: AWS re:Post
options.why: re:Post is a community Q&A service with answers from AWS experts and community members.

options.text: AWS Health Dashboard
options.why: The Health Dashboard reports service events.

options.text: AWS Artifact
options.why: Artifact provides compliance reports, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: AWS re:Post is a community-driven Q&A service where you can ask questions and get answers from the community and AWS experts.
explanation.concept: re:Post is available to all customers at no cost.
explanation.examTip: Ask the community = AWS re:Post.

stem: A company's EC2 instances in private subnets need to access Amazon S3 without traffic going through the internet.

options.text: An interface endpoint plus a NAT gateway
options.why: A NAT gateway sends traffic toward the internet, which the requirement forbids.

options.text: An internet gateway
options.why: An internet gateway routes traffic to the internet.

options.text: A VPC gateway endpoint for Amazon S3
options.why: Gateway endpoints route S3 traffic privately within the AWS network.

options.text: A public IP on each instance
options.why: Public IPs expose instances and use the internet.

explanation.answer: VPC endpoints let resources in a VPC reach supported AWS services privately. S3 and DynamoDB support gateway endpoints.
explanation.concept: Interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) support many other services.
explanation.examTip: Private access to S3/DynamoDB = gateway VPC endpoint.

stem: A company wants the strongest phishing-resistant MFA for its administrators.

options.text: Email codes
options.why: Email codes are not an IAM MFA option and are easier to phish.

options.text: SMS text message codes
options.why: AWS doesn't support SMS for IAM user MFA, and SMS is weaker.

options.text: A shared password written on a card
options.why: This isn't MFA and is insecure, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: FIDO2 security keys or passkeys
options.why: Passkeys and security keys are phishing-resistant MFA options supported by AWS.

explanation.answer: AWS supports passkeys and security keys (FIDO2), virtual authenticator apps and hardware TOTP tokens for MFA.
explanation.concept: FIDO2 security keys and passkeys resist phishing because they're bound to the website.
explanation.examTip: Strongest MFA = passkeys / FIDO2 security keys.

stem: A company sets up AWS Organizations. It wants to know the role of the management account.

options.text: It creates the org, manages accounts and pays the bill
options.why: The management account administers the organization and is responsible for billing.

options.text: It cannot invite or create other accounts
options.why: The management account invites and creates member accounts.

options.text: It hosts all production workloads for the organization
options.why: Best practice keeps workloads out of the management account.

options.text: It is restricted by SCPs like every member account
options.why: SCPs don't restrict the management account.

explanation.answer: The management account creates the organization, invites or creates member accounts, applies policies and pays for all accounts.
explanation.concept: Limit access to the management account and run workloads in member accounts.
explanation.examTip: Management account = admin + billing payer; keep workloads out.

stem: A startup asks whether it must pay for a public TLS certificate to use HTTPS on its CloudFront distribution.

options.text: Only Enterprise Support customers get free certificates
options.why: Support plans don't affect ACM pricing, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: No, ACM public certificates used with CloudFront are free
options.why: You pay only for the AWS resources that use the certificate.

options.text: Yes, ACM public certificates cost per month
options.why: Public certificates used with integrated services are free.

options.text: HTTPS isn't supported by CloudFront
options.why: CloudFront fully supports HTTPS, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

explanation.answer: Public SSL/TLS certificates provisioned through ACM are free for use with integrated services like CloudFront and Elastic Load Balancing.
explanation.concept: ACM handles renewal automatically.
explanation.examTip: ACM public certs with AWS services = free + auto-renew.

stem: A company wants to automatically isolate an EC2 instance when GuardDuty reports a high-severity finding about it.

options.text: A weekly manual review of GuardDuty findings
options.why: Manual weekly reviews are too slow for high-severity findings.

options.text: Turn off GuardDuty to stop the alerts
options.why: This removes detection, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Route findings via Amazon EventBridge to Lambda
options.why: EventBridge can trigger automated responses when findings arrive.

options.text: Email the findings to AWS Support for action
options.why: Support doesn't remediate your instances.

explanation.answer: GuardDuty findings are published to Amazon EventBridge, where rules can trigger Lambda functions or Systems Manager automation to respond.
explanation.concept: Automating responses is part of the security pillar ("prepare for security events").
explanation.examTip: Auto-respond to findings = EventBridge rule → Lambda/automation.

references.title: Processing GuardDuty findings with Amazon EventBridge

stem: A company uses Amazon RDS. A database engine security patch is released.

options.text: The customer must rebuild the database on EC2
options.why: That would remove the managed service benefits.

options.text: Patches are applied only when RDS is recreated
options.why: RDS applies patches during maintenance windows, not only on recreation.

options.text: The customer must SSH into the database host
options.why: RDS doesn't provide host OS access, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: AWS applies it during a maintenance window the customer can choose
options.why: RDS applies engine and OS patches during configured maintenance windows.

explanation.answer: With Amazon RDS, AWS handles patching. Customers choose a maintenance window and can schedule or apply updates.
explanation.concept: This shows shared responsibility: AWS patches, customers choose timing and test applications.
explanation.examTip: RDS patches = AWS applies in your maintenance window.

stem: A developer wants to test whether a new IAM policy allows a specific action before attaching it to production users.

options.text: The IAM policy simulator
options.why: The simulator tests and troubleshoots policies against specific actions and resources.

options.text: AWS CloudTrail Lake queries
options.why: CloudTrail shows past activity; it doesn't test a policy before it's attached.

options.text: Amazon Inspector
options.why: Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities.

options.text: AWS Pricing Calculator
options.why: The Pricing Calculator estimates costs, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: The IAM policy simulator lets you test the effects of identity-based policies, resource policies and SCPs before deploying them.
explanation.concept: Testing policies reduces the risk of over-granting or breaking access.
explanation.examTip: Test what a policy allows = IAM policy simulator.

references.title: Testing IAM policies with the IAM policy simulator

stem: A new engineer suggests creating access keys for the root user to run automation scripts.

options.text: Create root access keys only for CI/CD pipelines
options.why: Pipelines should use roles, not root credentials.

options.text: Don't create root access keys; use IAM roles or users with limited permissions
options.why: Root access keys have unrestricted access and are a major risk.

options.text: Create root access keys but store them in source code
options.why: Storing keys in code makes leaks more likely.

options.text: Create root access keys and rotate them yearly
options.why: Even rotated, root keys give unrestricted access.

explanation.answer: AWS recommends not creating access keys for the root user. Automation should use roles with least-privilege permissions.
explanation.concept: If root access keys exist, delete them.
explanation.examTip: Root access keys = don't.

stem: A company's licensing terms only allow its video service to be viewed in Canada.
prompt: Which AWS feature can block requests from other countries?

options.text: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode
options.why: Object Lock prevents deletion, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Security groups with country-based rules
options.why: Security groups don't filter by country.

options.text: Geo match in AWS WAF or CloudFront geo restriction
options.why: Both can allow or block requests by country.

options.text: Network ACLs with country-based rules
options.why: NACLs filter by IP range and port, not by country.

explanation.answer: AWS WAF geo match statements and CloudFront geographic restrictions can allow or block viewers based on their country.
explanation.concept: Geo-blocking supports licensing and compliance requirements.
explanation.examTip: Block by country = WAF geo match / CloudFront geo restriction.

references.title: Restricting the geographic distribution of your content

stem: A company with 50 accounts wants a single view of AWS Config compliance across all accounts and Regions.

options.text: A CloudFront distribution
options.why: CloudFront delivers content, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: One AWS Budgets report
options.why: Budgets track costs, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: AWS Trusted Advisor organizational view
options.why: Trusted Advisor's organizational view summarizes its own checks, not Config rule compliance.

options.text: An AWS Config aggregator
options.why: Aggregators collect Config data from multiple accounts and Regions into one view.

explanation.answer: An AWS Config aggregator collects configuration and compliance data from multiple accounts and Regions, including across an organization.
explanation.concept: Combine with conformance packs for organization-wide compliance.
explanation.examTip: Multi-account Config view = aggregator.

stem: A team building a shopping app asks whether customers should sign in as IAM users.

options.text: No, use Amazon Cognito for customer sign-in
options.why: Cognito is designed for app user identities at scale.

options.text: No, give customers the root user
options.why: Root credentials must never be shared, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: Yes, share one IAM user among all customers
options.why: Shared credentials are insecure, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Yes, create one IAM user per customer
options.why: IAM users are for access to your AWS account, not app customers.

explanation.answer: Amazon Cognito manages app users, sign-up, sign-in and federation with social and enterprise identity providers.
explanation.concept: IAM is for people and services that manage AWS resources.
explanation.examTip: App customers = Cognito. AWS administrators = IAM / Identity Center.

stem: A company asks which data stores Amazon Macie analyzes for sensitive data.

options.text: EC2 instance memory
options.why: Macie doesn't scan instance memory, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: Amazon S3 buckets
options.why: Macie discovers sensitive data in Amazon S3.

options.text: Amazon EBS volumes
options.why: Macie doesn't scan EBS volumes, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB tables
options.why: Macie analyzes S3; it doesn't scan DynamoDB tables.

explanation.answer: Amazon Macie automates sensitive data discovery in Amazon S3 and reports findings such as PII or financial data.
explanation.concept: Macie also assesses S3 bucket security and access controls.
explanation.examTip: Macie = S3 only.

stem: A company uses Amazon S3 to host files.
prompt: Which TWO are the company's responsibility? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Maintaining the storage servers behind S3
options.why: Hardware is AWS's responsibility, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: Replicating data within the S3 infrastructure for durability
options.why: AWS designs S3's internal redundancy, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: Deciding whether to use SSE-KMS and who can use the key
options.why: Encryption choices and key access are customer decisions.

options.text: Securing the facility that houses S3
options.why: Physical security is AWS's responsibility.

options.text: Setting bucket policies and access permissions
options.why: Access configuration is the customer's responsibility.

explanation.answer: For S3, customers manage access, encryption choices, data classification and versioning settings. AWS manages the infrastructure.
explanation.concept: Abstracted services still leave data and access decisions with the customer.
explanation.examTip: S3: you own access + encryption choices; AWS owns infrastructure + durability design.

stem: A manager asks the difference between an IAM user and an IAM role.

options.text: Users are for AWS services; roles are only for people
options.why: Roles are commonly used by services and people.

options.text: They are identical, with different names in the console
options.why: They differ in how credentials work, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: A user has long-term credentials; a role gives temporary ones
options.why: Roles provide temporary credentials to whoever is allowed to assume them.

options.text: A role has a permanent password; a user doesn't
options.why: Roles have no permanent password or access keys.

explanation.answer: IAM users are identities with long-term credentials. IAM roles have no long-term credentials; trusted entities assume them to get temporary credentials.
explanation.concept: AWS recommends roles and temporary credentials wherever possible.
explanation.examTip: User = long-term credentials. Role = temporary, assumed.

stem: Instances in a private subnet need to download software updates from the internet, but must not accept inbound connections from the internet.

options.text: An Elastic IP on each private instance
options.why: Public IPs would expose the instances, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: AWS Direct Connect
options.why: Direct Connect connects to on-premises networks, not the internet.

options.text: An internet gateway route in the private subnet
options.why: This would make the subnet public, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: A NAT gateway in a public subnet
options.why: A NAT gateway allows outbound internet access while blocking inbound connections.

explanation.answer: A NAT gateway lets instances in private subnets connect out to the internet while preventing the internet from initiating connections to them.
explanation.concept: NAT gateways are placed in public subnets and referenced in private route tables.
explanation.examTip: Private subnet needs outbound internet only = NAT gateway.

stem: A company already uses Trusted Advisor. Its security team now wants continuous checks against PCI DSS controls and aggregated findings from GuardDuty and Inspector.

options.text: AWS Security Hub
options.why: Security Hub runs standards like PCI DSS and aggregates findings from security services.

options.text: More Trusted Advisor checks
options.why: Trusted Advisor doesn't aggregate GuardDuty and Inspector findings or run PCI DSS standards.

options.text: AWS Budgets
options.why: Budgets track cost, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: AWS Artifact
options.why: Artifact provides AWS's reports, not checks on your resources.

explanation.answer: AWS Security Hub provides continuous checks against standards and centralizes findings from AWS security services and partners.
explanation.concept: Trusted Advisor gives broad best-practice recommendations; Security Hub is focused on security posture.
explanation.examTip: Security standards + aggregated findings = Security Hub.

stem: A security architect wants official AWS guidance on security best practices for designing workloads.

options.text: AWS Marketplace security product listings
options.why: Marketplace sells third-party software, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: The Well-Architected Framework Security pillar
options.why: It provides AWS's security best practices for workloads.

options.text: AWS Trusted Advisor security check results
options.why: Trusted Advisor flags specific risks in your account, but it isn't AWS's design guidance for building secure workloads.

options.text: The AWS Artifact SOC 2 report for AWS
options.why: Artifact reports describe AWS's controls, not how to design your workloads securely.

explanation.answer: The Well-Architected Security pillar describes security design principles and best practices, from identity to incident response.
explanation.concept: AWS also publishes security whitepapers, blogs and the Security Reference Architecture.
explanation.examTip: Official security design guidance = Well-Architected Security pillar.

stem: An operations lead is choosing services for monitoring and auditing.
prompt: Which TWO statements are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: CloudWatch can alarm on metrics like CPU usage
options.why: CloudWatch alarms watch metrics and trigger actions.

options.text: CloudTrail records who made API calls
options.why: CloudTrail logs API activity with the caller's identity.

options.text: CloudWatch encrypts S3 objects
options.why: CloudWatch is for monitoring, not encryption.

options.text: Config blocks DDoS attacks
options.why: Shield handles DDoS protection, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Artifact scans EC2 instances
options.why: Inspector scans instances, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

explanation.answer: CloudTrail = API auditing. CloudWatch = metrics, logs and alarms. Config = configuration history and compliance.
explanation.concept: These three services cover most monitoring and auditing questions.
explanation.examTip: CloudTrail (who), CloudWatch (how it's running), Config (what it looks like).
